# Market watch sweep

Run this once a week. The output is a set of atomic, sourced insights, a rewritten briefing page and one consolidated comment on the loop.

## 1. Build four working sets

**A. Competitors.** list_objects with type company and metadata_eq role=competitor. Page through all results. Skip any record whose metadata.lane is "duplicate". If the set is empty, build a starting list of 5 to 10 of the closest alternatives from web search and from what the workspace says about our product and buyers. Create each as a company with metadata.role=competitor, metadata.lane=weekly and a source link in its content, and list them in the consolidated comment so the workspace owner can confirm. This is the only case where you add competitors yourself.

**B. Rest of the category.** Companies and products in our space that are in neither A nor D. Find our space from the workspace's own positioning and strategy pages (search_objects with words such as positioning, strategy, category, customers).

**C. Customers and prospects.** Company objects with status customer or engaged (customers) and prospect (potential customers). Do not re-research each account. Read the insights filed on those companies in the last 7 days and the buyer segments in the workspace's customer or segment page (search_objects with words such as segments, ICP, target customers). Ask one question per segment: how is this buyer changing how they work, buy and spend on what we sell, and what moved this week? Use web search only to fill gaps at segment level, not account level.

**D. Learn-from products.** Products outside the competitor set that solve a related job well: adjacent products, consumer products, new entrants. Track them by name in the Learn-from section of the briefing page, and in their insights. Tier 3 (learn from) by default. Move one into set A only when it adds what makes it a direct rival. Do not set metadata.role=competitor on a product just to track it. For each, note what we can borrow: onboarding, memory, pricing, voice, trust model (permissions, approvals, credentials), plus anything else notable.

## 2. Size the work by lane (set A)

Every competitor record carries metadata.lane.
- **weekly**: full scan, as described in section 4.
- **light-weekly**: at most one line per product per week, and only when something changed (launch, price, funding). No line if nothing moved.
- **monthly**: skip in the weekly sweep except for a big move (funding, acquisition, pricing change, a launch that overlaps our core). The monthly revalidation covers the rest.
- **quarterly**: checked once a quarter, in the first monthly run of January, April, July and October.
- **duplicate**: never swept.
A record with no lane is treated as quarterly. Flag it in the consolidated comment so someone sets the lane.

Price cuts by model or infrastructure vendors fold into one pricing storyline on the briefing page, not a separate insight each time. Publishers of "best tools" lists go to whoever owns search content in this workspace, if anyone does. Otherwise skip them.

## 3. Watch topics

The briefing page has a **Watch topics** line: segments or phrase sets worth a weekly look without becoming competitors, such as a new adjacent segment or funded rivals who avoid our words. Search each with widened phrases. File an insight only for a real move. Do not set metadata.role=competitor on anything found this way; changes to the list go through the monthly revalidation. If the line is empty, propose two topics in the next monthly revalidation.

## 4. What to scan

For sets A, B and D, scan the last 7 days with web search and page fetch. Look for product launches, feature or roadmap changes, pricing, press releases, executive moves and notable hires, company social posts, annual or reporting results, funding rounds, new entrants, analyst and community sentiment shifts, and positioning moves. Prefer primary sources. Confirm anything important with a second source.

## 5. Read every lane, not only this loop's

Other agents file market-relevant insights outside this loop (intake, community listening, search research, ad hoc research briefs). Before you write the briefing page, list_objects with type insight and updated_after set to 30 days ago, page through all results, and pick out everything about competitors, learn-from products, the category, vendors' launches and pricing, and buyers. A big move that another lane already filed MUST appear on the briefing page even if you did not find it in this week's scan. Link those insights. Do not refile them.

## 6. Lane assignment rule

- A finding about any company in the competitor set goes in the Competitor lane, however category-shaping it feels.
- A finding about a learn-from product goes in the Learn-from lane, unless that company is also in the competitor set. Then it goes in the Competitor lane and still gets a "What we can learn" line.
- The Category lane is strictly for companies in neither set.
- When in doubt, check the competitor list first.
- Do not filter out large vendors that target our slot. Those are exactly what the workspace owner wants to see.
- Customer and prospect findings that the account sweep already filed are linked, not refiled. A segment-level customer finding nobody has filed gets one insight tagged ['customer-direction', '<segment-slug>'].

## 7. Insight schema (clustering depends on it)

- metadata.tags is a JSON array of strings, never a comma-separated string.
- Competitor lane: exactly ['competitor-intel', '<company-slug>'] (company slug lowercase, hyphenated).
- Learn-from lane: exactly ['learn-from-intel', '<product-slug>']. The content ends with a line starting **What we can learn:** and a line **Tier:** 3 (learn from) or 1 (adds what makes it a direct rival).
- Category lane: ['market-direction'] plus up to 3 theme tags.
- Every insight carries a source link, the date, the source type and a confidence line (High, Medium or Low).
- Link to the company with an informs edge when one applies. In the Competitor lane, also update the company object's content with any material, dated, sourced benchmark line.
- Dedup first with search_objects. Update instead of duplicating.
- Do not file noise, and do not file chatter about this workspace's own agents, loops, triggers or prompts.

## 8. Loop hygiene

Find the loop with list_loops (its name is Market & Competitor Watch). Every insight you file must be linked into it with an in_loop relationship (source the loop, target the insight). Create the edge with update_objects edges at creation time. For an existing insight you update, check list_relationships (source_id the loop, type in_loop) first and skip if the edge is there.

## 9. Link integrity

Use the url field returned by the tools verbatim when you link an insight, bet or company. Never retype an id by hand. Before posting, run get_objects on every id you are about to link and fix any url that does not resolve.

## 10. Briefing page, urgent items, consolidated comment

1. Load the skill **market-briefing-page** and rewrite the briefing page. This is required every week, including quiet ones.
2. For each Act now item on the page, post one comment on the loop right away: attention 5 if it blocks something this week, otherwise 4. @mention the workspace owner (a human; find them with list_actors). Put the ask on line 2 and link the briefing page. If a storyline changes the long-term picture, also @mention the Market Strategist on the briefing page with one line, so the outlook page is refreshed ahead of the monthly cycle.
3. Post ONE consolidated comment on the loop. Line 1 is a one-line headline linking the briefing page. Then exactly four labelled sections: **Competitor set**, **Learn-from products**, **Rest of category**, **Customers and prospects**. One line per item with its link. Learn-from lines end with the thing to borrow. @mention only for genuinely material items. Attention 4 only for a truly material move (a material launch, funding round, hire, pivot or a near-term threat to us). Otherwise attention 2. If nothing is notable in any lane, skip the comment. The page is still rewritten.

# Market briefing page

You are the only editor of one living knowledge object titled **Market briefing: what happened and what it means**. Find it with search_objects. If it does not exist yet, create it with status draft, with an intro paragraph that names the scope and has a "Last updated" date. The scope reads: competitors, learn-from products, the wider category, and our customers and prospects.

The long-term companion, **Market outlook and positioning**, belongs to the Market Strategist. Never edit it.

## Setup, every week

1. Make sure the briefing page is linked into the loop (list_loops, name Market & Competitor Watch) with an in_loop relationship (source the loop, target the page). Check with list_relationships first and create it with update_objects edges only if missing.
2. Read the page first. Keep what is still true and replace what is stale. Rewrite the whole page each week. Never append a second copy.
3. When the page has real content for the first time, set its status to validated and put today's date in the "Last updated" line. Leave it validated after that.

## Sections, in this order

1. **Quick read**: at most 8 lines, readable in 30 seconds. One sentence verdict on the month. The 3 biggest shifts, one line each, each linked to its storyline. The threat level (Low, Medium or High) and since when. What it means for us in one line. If you cannot find our positioning or target segments in the workspace, add one line: "Missing: <what>, needed from <who>". Repeat that line every week until it is closed.
2. **Act now**: only items that need a reaction this week. Each says what happened, who reacts (agent or human) and by when. Otherwise write "Nothing urgent."
3. **The last 30 days: the big storylines**: 3 or 4 storylines, biggest first. A storyline is a group of moves that belong together (one vendor launches and the others respond within days), not a list of press releases. Each has a bold one-line title and these parts: **What happened** (dated, 2 to 3 lines), **Who reacted and how fast** (name each vendor and the day gap), **What it shows about where the market is going**, **So what for us**, and a link to its deep-dive. If a learn-from product is involved, add a **What we can learn** line.
4. **This week's moves**: four short lists (Competitors, Learn-from products, Category, Customers and prospects). One line each, dated, linked, with our read. Each list opens with a bold takeaway. Learn-from lines end with what we can borrow.
5. **Passed to the strategist**: findings that confirm or challenge the long-term view, one line each with a link.
6. **Watch next**: two to four concrete things to check next week. Include the **Watch topics** line the sweep reads (see the market-watch-sweep skill).
7. **Last four weeks at a glance**: one line per week. Move last week's quick-read verdict down here and drop the oldest line so only four remain.

## Readability rules (hard)

- Glanceable first, deep detail one click down.
- Every section except Quick read opens with ONE bold takeaway line. No section is longer than about 12 lines. Anything longer moves into a linked deep-dive page.
- Plain English a non-technical founder can read in two minutes: no em-dashes, no backticks, no jargon without a short gloss. Use bold for names and fields. Every object you name is a markdown link using the url returned by the tools.
- Numbers need a unit and a comparison (against last week, against target). Say plainly when a sample is too small.

## Storyline deep-dive pages

For each storyline keep a knowledge object titled **Storyline: <name> (<month year>)** with the full timeline, sources, vendor-by-vendor detail and your confidence. Create it with status draft if missing, update it if it exists. Link it to the briefing page with a relates_to edge and into the loop with an in_loop edge. Drop a storyline from the page once it is older than 45 days and nothing new has happened, but keep its deep-dive page.

## Threat level

State it as Low, Medium or High, with the date it last changed.
- **Low**: no competitor or category move this month touches who we sell to, what we claim or what we price.
- **Medium**: at least one move overlaps one of those three, but no customer or prospect has raised it and nothing forces a change this month.
- **High**: a move directly changes who we sell to, what we claim or what we price, or customers and prospects are already raising it. It needs a reaction this week.

## Each week's question

Each week the page answers one question: did a market move change who we sell to, what we claim, or what we price?

# Competitor list review

Run this once a month. You propose, a human decides. Do NOT add, remove or re-role companies yourself. Setting or fixing metadata.lane is allowed and is not a list change.

## A. Competitor list revalidation

Re-derive the set: list_objects with type company and metadata_eq role=competitor, paging through all results and skipping records whose metadata.lane is "duplicate". With web search and page fetch, produce three sections:
- **ADD**: a new or newly significant competitor or category entrant from the last 30 days that should join, including a company the workspace already tracks under a different role. Give the source and date.
- **DROP**: any current competitor that looks dead, defunct, pivoted or merged, with a credible source and date.
- **CORRECT**: renames, role mistags, lane mistags and other list corrections.

Give the monthly lane its pass here: one line per record only when something changed since last month (release, price, funding, team features). Records in the quarterly lane are checked in the first monthly run of each quarter (January, April, July, October).

## B. Category scope revalidation

Ask which category signals the weekly sweep is systematically missing or over-covering. Propose specific tracking-scope adjustments, for example "add a fourth sub-segment" or "drop generic tool chatter". Include the Watch topics from the briefing page and say whether their search phrases still catch the moves. If the Watch topics line is empty, propose two.

## C. Regulation check

Search for changes in the last 30 days to laws, standards, guidance or enforcement that touch what we sell or how our buyers use it. The briefing page's Watch topics line names the rules to follow; if it names none, pick the ones that apply to our category from the workspace's positioning pages. Report one line with the primary source link if something changed, otherwise one line "no change".

## Output

Post ONE comment on the loop (find it with list_loops, name Market & Competitor Watch) with the sections above. @mention the workspace owner (a human; find them with list_actors) to confirm the list changes. Attention 2 by default. Attention 4 only if a competitor materially disappeared, a new near-term threat emerged, or the scope gap is significant.

# Market outlook page

You are the sole owner of one living knowledge object titled **Market outlook and positioning: where we are heading and are we doing the right things**. The Market Researcher owns the short-term companion, **Market briefing: what happened and what it means**. Read it and never edit it.

This page is the long view. It covers where the market is heading and where our customers and prospects are heading, and why. It says whether we are doing the right things, how we should position and react, and how we can be proactive. The aim is to be one year ahead and, ideally, to know where things move in three years. It is for getting ahead of the market, not for urgent news.

## First step

Make sure this page is linked into the loop (list_loops, name Market & Competitor Watch) with an in_loop relationship (source the loop, target the page). Check with list_relationships first and create it with update_objects edges only if missing. If the page does not exist, create it with status draft.

## Inputs

The briefing page and its "Passed to the strategist" section. The storyline pages it links. The last four weekly sweep comments on the loop. Competitor-intel, market-direction, customer-direction and other market insights from the last 30 to 90 days. Customer account insights. The competitor list and its company pages. Our own strategy, positioning and customer pages, and the bets in flight (search_objects). If a market fact is missing, ask the Market Researcher (create_session with wait true when you need it in this session, or an @mention). Do not ask a human for a fact.

## Sections, in this order

Rewrite the whole page each month. Keep what is still true, replace what is stale, and where a section did not change write "Reviewed <date>, no change".

1. **Quick read**: at most 8 lines, readable in 30 seconds. A one-sentence verdict: are we on the right course? The 2 or 3 directions the market is moving in. Ready, React or Get ahead for each. The single most important move.
2. **Where the market is heading, and why**: bold takeaway first. Two or three directions only. For each: the direction in one line, the force behind it (cost, buyer pressure, regulation, technology), 2 to 3 linked pieces of evidence, and confidence (High, Medium or Low).
3. **Where our customers and prospects are heading, and why**: same shape, for the buyer segments and the named customers and prospects who carry the most weight. Link their company objects. Say what they are changing in how they work, buy and spend.
4. **Are we doing the right things?**: bold takeaway first. A short table of our live and define-stage bets and positioning claims against the directions above, marked Right course, Adjust or Missing. Link each bet. Mark uncovered directions "Gap: no bet". Do not create bets yourself. If a gap matters, say so in your comment to the workspace owner.
5. **How we should position and react**: bold takeaway first. Per direction: Ready, React or Get ahead; the move; who owns it; by when. Include what we should do proactively, not only defensively.
6. **One year ahead**: the 3 to 5 capabilities, positioning claims or bets we need to hold in twelve months to still be a year ahead. Link the bet that covers each.
7. **Three years out**: your view of the industry in three years, five lines at most, with confidence and the two or three conditions that would change it. Mark opinion versus sourced.
8. **Open questions**: what you could not source, and who is asked.

## Readability rules (hard)

Every section opens with one bold takeaway line. No section is longer than about 12 lines. Push detail into a linked knowledge page. Plain English a non-technical founder can read in two minutes: no em-dashes, no backticks, no jargon without a short gloss, bold for names, every object named is a markdown link using the url from the tools, no horizontal rules.

## Finish

Set the intro "Last updated" to today. When the page has real content for the first time, set its status to validated and leave it validated after that. Then post ONE comment on the page. Line 1 is the single biggest shift since last month (20 words at most). Line 2 is the ask, or "No ask". @mention the workspace owner (a human; find them with list_actors) only if a direction means a real pivot call or a Get ahead item needs their decision. Attention 3 by default, 4 only for a live pivot question. Also refresh the page ahead of schedule when the Market Researcher @mentions you on the briefing page that a storyline changes the long-term picture.
